meta.subtitle: Second-quarter 2026 results met or beat guidance, but guided growth slows and the shares sit near their 52-week low

advisories: model vs Street expected return diverge by 25pp — informational, not scored

analystSentiment.commentary:
Boston Scientific Corporation's second quarter of 2026 met or beat its own guidance, yet the shares trade at $42.26, near the bottom of their 52-week range. We hold back from a positive call for three reasons: the company's July 29, 2026 outlook points to slower growth, its 10-Q reports increased competition in Electrophysiology and a deceleration of certain WATCHMAN procedures, and the risks section sets out why the fall in the share price may mean consensus is too high.

Our scenarios put the weighted value close to the current price, with a Bear case well below it, and that derives HOLD. The call is close on the weights: a moderate shift from Bear to Bull would derive BUY, and the valuation section argues why we do not make it. The final recommendation sets out the price and the third-quarter evidence that would change the label.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Boston Scientific Corporation describes itself in its 10-Q as "a global developer, manufacturer and marketer of medical devices that are used in a broad range of interventional medical specialties". It is headquartered in Marlborough, Massachusetts.

The 10-Q MD&A presents net sales by two reportable segments. MedSurg comprises the Endoscopy, Urology and Neuromodulation businesses. Cardiovascular has, since the fourth quarter of 2025, combined the legacy Cardiology and Peripheral Interventions businesses. Its products include the Farapulse Pulsed Field Ablation (PFA) System, the AGENT Drug-Coated Balloon and, in the company description in our data, WATCHMAN FLX, a left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) device. Cardiovascular is the larger segment, with second-quarter 2026 net sales of $3,624 million against $1,818 million for MedSurg.

In the second quarter of 2026, which ended June 30, net sales were $5.442 billion, up 7.5% year over year on a reported basis and 7.0% on an organic basis. Reported diluted EPS was $0.61, against $0.53 a year earlier.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: The case turns on whether FY27 consensus earnings hold through the slowdown the company has guided to. If they do, the current price pays a low multiple for a business with high gross margins, strong free cash flow and an active clinical program. If they do not, the multiple is less low than it looks. We think consensus is more likely to hold than to break, but not by enough to pay for a re-rating, so our Base keeps today's multiple and our Bear prices the shares on reported earnings. The catalysts and risks below point to the evidence that would tip the balance.

catalysts: The third-quarter 2026 report will test the company's guidance for approximately 3 to 5 percent reported and organic net sales growth and adjusted EPS of $0.80 to $0.82.
Delivery on the company's full-year adjusted EPS guidance, which sits above the Street's FY26 mean, would raise the base from which FY27 estimates start.
Clinical results the July 29 release reports, including the AVANT GUARD study of FARAPULSE in persistent atrial fibrillation, could support demand if they translate into adoption.
The new global restructuring program the Board approved on July 21, 2026 may lower costs.
A decision on the exclusive option to acquire the MiRus TAVR business, whose SIEGEL system is investigational, would show what the $1.5 billion MiRus stake is meant to deliver.
risks: The 10-Q reports increased competition in Electrophysiology and a deceleration of certain WATCHMAN procedures in the second quarter.
The market may be pricing a deterioration that the filings have not yet shown.
Tariff and trade policy uncertainty could raise costs and reverse part of the second-quarter gross margin gain.
Urology growth was relatively flat, and procurement pressure in China may spread beyond the stone franchise.
Street estimates sit on adjusted EPS, which excludes charges that are large in the reported accounts.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Revenue grew from $11.9B in FY21 to $20.1B in FY25, quickening every year to +19.9% in FY25, while operating margin widened from 10.1% to 18.0% and diluted EPS reached $1.94. The five years show operating leverage, despite a dip in FY24.

The second quarter of 2026 lifted gross margin to 70.7% from 67.7% a year earlier, but most of the gain sat outside pricing, volume and mix. The 10-Q's reconciliation credits 0.6% to "Sales pricing, volume and mix", deducts 0.4% for currency, and credits 2.9% to "All other, including inventory charges and other period expenses". Its text names higher-margin product sales, "the recovery of previously incurred tariffs" and "a decrease in inventory charges" as the primary factors. We expect the mix benefit to last and the tariff recovery and inventory items not to repeat at the same size, so we look for gross margin nearer the FY25 level of 69.0% than the second-quarter figure. Operating income was $1,178 million against $819 million, a 21.6% margin, with SG&A and R&D both lower as a share of net sales.

Net income attributable to common stockholders rose 13.8% to $907 million, an increase the 10-Q says was "primarily driven by higher net sales". The income statement also shows "Other, net" swinging from income of $213 million to an expense of $23 million, which held net income growth well below operating income growth. Over the six months to June 30, reported diluted EPS of $1.51 against $0.98 includes "a discrete tax benefit recorded in the first quarter of 2026", so the half-year GAAP growth overstates the trend.

Adjusted EPS, a non-GAAP measure, was $0.86 against $0.75. The 10-Q says its adjusted measures "exclude certain charges and/or credits" reported in GAAP net income "for purposes of assessing operating performance" and lists amortization expense among the expenses management excludes; the release adds intangible asset impairment, acquisition-related, restructuring and restructuring-related, and litigation-related charges among items it is "unable to predict with reasonable certainty". Second-quarter adjusted net income of $1,275 million, set beside reported net income, shows the exclusions are large, so we use GAAP figures for the record and adjusted EPS only as the basis of Street estimates and guidance.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary:
At December 31, 2025, the end of FY25, the company held $2.0B of cash and short-term investments against total debt of $11.4B, leaving net debt of $9.5B, with total equity of $24.5B.

Leverage appears to have risen since then. Year-end net debt set against FY25 EBITDA of $5.0B gives a lower ratio than the 2.2x on the trailing-twelve-month line, even though trailing margins are higher than FY25's on higher revenue, which points to net debt above the year-end level. The current ratio fits that reading: 1.62 at FY25 and 1.24 on the trailing line. The completed accelerated share repurchase and the MiRus investment, both reported in the July 29 release, each required cash and are consistent with the rise.

The balance sheet still does not constrain the thesis. At the trailing ratio, and with interest coverage of 11.4x, the company has room for a further commitment on the scale of the MiRus stake, which would be smaller than one year of the free cash flow discussed below. The year-end figures, however, now overstate the cushion.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Operating cash flow rose from $1.9B in FY21 to $4.5B in FY25, and free cash flow from $1.3B to $3.7B, as the FCF margin widened to 18.2%. Capital expenditure stayed between $0.6B and $0.9B a year, so most of the gain in operating cash flow reached free cash flow. At the current price the trailing free cash flow yield is 5.9%, a solid return for a business that turns more than its net income into free cash flow.

The dividend yield is 0.00% today, and the table shows only small dividend payments in its early years, so cash returns now come through the buyback discussed under capital allocation.

The FCF margin widened in years when revenue growth quickened, and we expect it to hold up less well in the slower years the growth section describes, so we do not treat the trailing yield as a floor under the price.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
At $42.26 the shares trade on 17.1x trailing earnings, 13.2x trailing EV/EBITDA and 2.9x sales, within a 52-week range of $41.94 to $105.65. The trailing P/E lines up with reported diluted EPS over the four quarters to June 30, 2026, a window that includes the discrete tax benefit of early 2026, so the multiple looks lower than it would on earnings without that benefit.

The forward multiples sit on a different basis. The vendor's 13.0x "NTM" P/E lines up with the FY26 consensus EPS of $3.26, so it is in effect a current-year multiple, and the 12.4x figure lines up with the FY27 consensus of $3.40. The FY26 consensus sits close to, and just below, the company's July 29, 2026 guidance for 2026 adjusted EPS of $3.28 to $3.32, so we read the consensus figures as adjusted, non-GAAP estimates, on the definition set out in the financials section.

The Street is more positive than we are. Of 31 analysts, 25 rate the shares Buy, 6 Hold and none Sell. The consensus target is $60.62 and the median $60.00, within a range of $44.00 to $94.00, so even the lowest target sits above the current price. Our data does not date these targets.

On these multiples the shares are inexpensive if FY27 consensus holds, and the scenarios below price what happens if it does not.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Third-quarter organic growth comes in above the top of the company's range, the full-year adjusted EPS range is held or raised, and Electrophysiology growth holds up against increased competition. The market then moves to the Street's median target of $60.00, a Street figure rather than a multiple of our own.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Third-quarter growth lands within the company's range and FY27 consensus holds: EPS of $3.40 at 13.0x, the current-year multiple the market pays today, rolled forward a year. Growth follows FY27 consensus, and the multiple neither expands nor contracts.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Increased Electrophysiology competition and the WATCHMAN deceleration carry into FY27, adjusted EPS growth stalls, and charges from the new restructuring program weigh on reported results. The market then values the shares on reported earnings: diluted EPS no higher than FY25's $1.94, at today's trailing 17.1x. That applies the trailing multiple to lower earnings than the trailing window holds, and on the Street's adjusted FY26 estimate it is a much lower multiple than the Base's.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
All three anchors depend on FY27 earnings. The page has no FY27 data beyond consensus, so we weight the scenarios on the most recent evidence about the path into that year, and it points both ways.

The Base carries 55%. FY27 consensus looks achievable: it asks for only modest growth over FY26, as the growth section shows, and the Street's FY26 figure already sits below the company's own guided range, as noted above. The evidence set out for the Bear and the Bull below cuts both ways, so the Base is the midpoint, and it keeps today's multiple.

The Bear carries 25%. Its condition is that the pressures the 10-Q reports in Cardiovascular carry into FY27, and the company's own third-quarter outlook, a step down from the second quarter, is the evidence that they have not yet eased. The new restructuring program, discussed under capital allocation, adds reported charges that bear directly on this scenario's anchor. Against it, Electrophysiology was still a primary growth driver in the second quarter, so the evidence so far shows slower growth rather than decline (see risks).

The Bull carries 20%, less than the Bear. Its condition, third-quarter growth above the top of the range, is plausible: the second quarter landed at or above the top of guidance (see leadership), and the Street's targets support the Bull's price. It also needs a large re-rating within a year, which one quarter of evidence does not yet justify.

These weights give a probability-weighted fair value of $44.60. The call is close on the split. Swapping the Bull and Bear weights leaves the label at HOLD, but moving about ten points from Bear to Bull would derive BUY. We do not make that move because the company's third-quarter outlook, cited above for the Bear, is its most recent statement on growth; a reader who gives more weight to the evidence cited for the Base and the Bull would reach BUY. SELL is further away: no shift of similar size toward the Bear reaches it at today's price.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Our data vendor shows only a consolidated total and treats the company as a single segment, while the 10-Q MD&A and the July 29 release present net sales by two reportable segments, MedSurg and Cardiovascular; we use the company's presentation. In the second quarter of 2026, Cardiovascular net sales grew 8.3% on a reported basis and MedSurg 5.9%, within which Neuromodulation rose 12.7%, Endoscopy 7.6% and Urology 1.1%. With the larger segment also growing faster, the company's growth depends most on Cardiovascular, and the MedSurg businesses cushion rather than replace it.

moatFactors.name: Clinical evidence and approvals
moatFactors.body: Device sales depend on clinical data and regulatory clearance, and the company keeps producing both. The July 29 release reports that the AVANT GUARD study "demonstrated statistical superiority of FARAPULSE PFA over anti-arrhythmic drugs" and that the FRACTURE trial "met its primary endpoints", and it reports a 510(k) clearance for the TruSelect 2.6 Microcatheter. The 10-K risk factors, filed February 17, 2026, warn that a delay in next-generation launches, or a loss of "continued physician confidence in" those products, "may result in declines in our market share", so the advantage has to be renewed product by product.

moatFactors.name: Gross margin stability
moatFactors.body: Gross margin held between 68.6% and 69.5% from FY21 to FY25 while revenue grew every year, which suggests growth has not come at the cost of margin. We rest the factor on that five-year range: the 10-Q's bridge groups pricing with volume and mix, so it cannot isolate pricing, and the trailing 69.9% includes second-quarter items, such as the tariff recovery, that may not recur. The 10-K warns of "national and regional government tenders", and the 10-Q reports volume-based procurement in China weighing on the stone franchise, so the strength is not uniform across products.

moatFactors.name: R&D scale and breadth
moatFactors.body: R&D expenses were $554 million in the second quarter of 2026, or 10.2% of net sales. They rose $28 million, an increase the 10-Q attributes primarily to investments "in order to maintain a pipeline of products that we believe will contribute to future sales growth". Four businesses spread the risk of any one product. The 10-K counters that "some of our competitors may have greater financial and marketing resources than we do" and that developments by other companies, "including low-cost alternatives, may make our products or proposed products obsolete or less competitive". We rate the factor moderate because spending at this scale helps but does not guarantee the next product.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat narrow. The case for an advantage rests on the five-year margin history and the clinical programs described above. The case against comes from the company's own filings: the 10-Q reports increased competition in Electrophysiology, and the 10-K describes markets that are "highly competitive" and "characterized by extensive research and development and rapid technological change". A wide rating would need evidence that the company can hold its position in Electrophysiology as competition increases, and one quarter of continued growth there is not yet that evidence. Durability over the next few years depends on whether the investigational products discussed under growth reach the market and sell.

points: Guidance implies a slower second half. On July 29, 2026 the company said it "now estimates" full-year 2026 net sales growth of approximately 5.5 to 6.5 percent reported and 5 to 6 percent organic, after organic growth of 8.1% in the six months to June 30. Its third-quarter outlook is approximately 3 to 5 percent on a reported and organic basis, a step down from the second quarter's pace.

Consensus expects a lower pace in FY27 as well. Consensus revenue of $21.2B (+6%) for FY26 sits inside the company's range, and $22.3B for FY27 implies growth well below the FY25 acceleration covered in the financials section. Consensus EPS of $3.40 for FY27 is only modestly above the $3.26 expected for FY26.

Cardiovascular's growth drivers face increased competition. The 10-Q credits the segment's second-quarter growth primarily to its coronary therapies franchise, led by the AGENT Drug-Coated Balloon, and to its Electrophysiology business unit, led by Farapulse. The competition and deceleration it reports in the same segment, discussed under risks, limit how much of that growth we carry into FY27.

Neuromodulation and Endoscopy add breadth. The 10-Q credits Neuromodulation's growth primarily to its pain portfolio, led by the Intracept Intraosseous Nerve Ablation System and the Nalu Peripheral Nerve Stimulation System, and to deep brain stimulation, and Endoscopy's to its biliary franchise, led by the AXIOS Stent and Delivery System, and its core GI franchise. Neither paragraph in the 10-Q mentions competitive pressure, which makes them the steadier contributors for now.

The pipeline is optionality, not a support for FY27. The July 29 release lists three investigational devices as "Not available for sale": the FARAFLEX Mapping and PFA Catheter, for which it says enrollment had commenced in the pivotal FARADIGM trial, the SEISMIQ 4CE Coronary Intravascular Lithotripsy Catheter and the SIEGEL TAVR system. Until they are cleared for sale we give them no weight in FY27 earnings.

management.leadership: The July 29, 2026 release names Mike Mahoney as chairman and chief executive officer; the proxy excerpt of March 18, 2026 calls Mr. Mahoney "our President and Chief Executive Officer". His comment on the quarter was measured, describing "a solid quarter while continuing to navigate a dynamic environment" and a focus on "disciplined execution and prioritizing investments in our highest-impact opportunities". The quarter landed at or above the top of guidance: reported growth of 7.5% against a range of 5.5 to 7.5 percent, organic growth of 7.0% against 5 to 7 percent, and adjusted EPS of $0.86 against $0.82 to $0.84. That fits a team that guides conservatively, which, if it holds, makes the third-quarter range more likely to be met or beaten, though one quarter cannot establish a pattern.
management.capitalAllocation:
Recent capital has gone to a buyback, a minority stake and restructuring. The July 29, 2026 release reports completion of the previously announced $2 billion accelerated share repurchase program, "repurchasing approximately 40 million shares", and those two figures put the average price paid above today's $42.26. The per-share benefit is real and shows in diluted weighted-average shares of 1,474.8 million in the second quarter, down from 1,493.5 million a year earlier. But the company paid more than the market now asks, and together with the MiRus payment the buyback is consistent with the rise in leverage the financials section describes.

The $1.5 billion MiRus LLC investment bought an approximately 34% equity stake and an exclusive option to acquire the MiRus TAVR business. Its return depends on an investigational TAVR system and an acquisition decision still to come, so we treat it as unproven.

On July 21, 2026 the Board approved a new global restructuring program. The activities of its predecessor, the 2023 Restructuring Plan, were "substantially complete at the end of 2025", in the 10-Q's words, with $748 million of cumulative pre-tax charges, within an estimated total of approximately $700 million to $800 million. If the new program resembles it, reported charges are likely through FY27 before savings show, so we give it no credit for savings.
management.governance: The proxy statement excerpt (DEF 14A, March 18, 2026) shows that the Board has determined that, other than Mr. Mahoney, all directors qualify as independent under NYSE standards, and that the Corporate Governance Guidelines require "a significant majority" of independent directors. Related party transactions fall under a written policy overseen by the Nominating and Governance Committee, with the General Counsel identifying potential transactions and providing an annual summary; the policy covers transactions above the SEC disclosure threshold, generally $120,000. The excerpt carries no executive pay detail, so we make no claim about pay design. For shareholders, a board that is independent apart from the chief executive and a written related-party process are a sound base. The gap is that Mr. Mahoney holds both the chair and chief executive titles set out in leadership, and the excerpt does not show whether a lead independent director balances that.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt we draw on contains no beneficial ownership table, so we make no statement about how much stock directors and officers hold.

idiosyncratic: Electrophysiology and WATCHMAN. The 10-Q says second-quarter and first-half net sales "were impacted by increased competition within our Electrophysiology business unit and a deceleration of certain WATCHMAN procedures". The same 10-Q still credits Electrophysiology, led by Farapulse, as a primary driver of growth in both periods, and limits the WATCHMAN point to "certain" procedures, so the evidence shows slower growth, not decline. That is still enough to matter: slower growth in a unit the 10-Q credits with the company's growth is the most direct route to the stalled earnings our Bear assumes.

An unexplained fall. The shares sit near their 52-week low, and none of the excerpts we draw on, from the 10-Q, the July 29 release, the 10-K and the proxy statement, gives a reason. The market may be pricing later information, including anything that followed the 10-Q of August 3, 2026. If its caution proves right, FY27 consensus may be too high, and so would our Base, which rests on it; we treat that as a risk to the estimates rather than as a reason to raise the Bear weight.

Adjusted versus reported earnings. Guidance and Street estimates sit on adjusted EPS, and the gap to reported earnings set out in the financials section is wide. Restructuring charges are among the items adjusted EPS excludes, so the new program discussed under capital allocation is likely to widen that gap, and an investor who values the company on reported earnings pays a higher multiple than the forward P/E suggests. Our Bear prices that shift in basis.

Urology and procurement. The 10-Q attributes Urology's "relatively flat" growth primarily to "underperformance in our stone franchise as a result of volume-based-procurement in China" and to commercial disruption in sacral neuromodulation. The 10-K warns that local procurement processes "may favor local players to multinational companies like us", so the pressure could reach other products.
risks.systemic:
Trade policy is the systemic risk the 10-Q stresses. It describes "significant uncertainty with respect to global trade policies, including changing tariff rates", which "could adversely impact our operations and results", and says the company "may also experience higher distribution costs and supply chain disruptions". The tariff recovery that lifted second-quarter gross margin, set out in the financials section, shows the same policies can move margins in either direction.

Across the industry, the 10-K risk factors filed February 17, 2026 point to consolidation among customers, government tenders and shifts in sites of care that "may impact procedure volumes, product mix, and pricing and contracting". These are slow-moving pressures, while tariffs are the one that could move margins within a year.

body: We rate Boston Scientific HOLD with a target range of $40.00 to $47.00, which brackets our Base of $44.20 and our weighted fair value. For a holder, a weighted value close to the price and a bear case well below it argue for neither adding nor selling. For a buyer, the Street's more positive view is the opposing case, and we would come round to it on a lower price or on the third-quarter evidence set out below.

With our scenarios unchanged, the label moves with the price: at the bottom of our range the page's math derives BUY, and at the top it derives SELL. The third-quarter report is the evidence that would move the weights. Organic growth above the top of the company's third-quarter range, with the full-year adjusted EPS range held or raised, would meet the Bull's condition and, in our view, justify moving about ten points from Bear to Bull, which narrowly derives BUY at today's price. Growth below the range, or a cut to the full-year range, would put the FY27 consensus behind our Base at risk and move weight to the Bear; that would lower our weighted value, though at today's price it would also take a lower Base to reach SELL.
